steps.title: The Professional Open
steps.content:
Hi, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. Is {{contact_first_name}} available, please?

Hi {{contact_first_name}}, the reason I'm calling is that we're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and we came across yours. {{asked_by}} check in on your home's plumbing and make sure everything's still doing what it should. Do you have a quick minute?

steps.title: The Opening Question
steps.content:
So {{contact_first_name}}, how has the plumbing been treating you since we were last out? Is everything still running great, is it starting to act up a little, or are you having real problems with it?

(This question has only three possible answers. Click the one you hear.)

steps.title: It’s Still Running Great
steps.content:
That's great to hear, {{contact_first_name}}. That's exactly what we like to hear.

Let me ask you this while I have you: when was the last time the plumbing was actually looked at or serviced? Was it recently, has it been a while, or are you not really sure?

steps.title: It’s Starting to Act Up
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I appreciate you telling me that, and honestly, that does happen over time. The good news is you caught it while it's still a little thing, and little things are a whole lot easier to deal with than big ones.

(Let them respond.)

steps.title: They’re Having Real Problems
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I'm sorry to hear that. That's frustrating, and I'm glad we called when we did. What's been going on?

Let them answer. Be empathetic and listen. Do NOT try to book anything yet. If they describe sewage backing up, a major active leak, flooding, or a gas smell, use the URGENT button.

steps.title: Serviced Recently: Stay Ahead of It
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, that's fantastic. You're doing exactly what most people don't, and it's why everything is still running great.

Let me ask you one more thing: even with everything running well, are you noticing any little early signs? A drain that’s gotten slow, a faucet that drips, hot water that runs out faster than it used to. Anything you'd want to stay ahead of?

steps.title: It’s Been a While
steps.content:
About how long would you say?

Let them answer.

That's really common. Plumbing just quietly does its job, so it's easy for time to get away from you.

Can I share why I ask? (Wait for their response.)

The longer plumbing goes without being looked at, the more likely there's something small waiting to be found. A worn valve, a slow drip, a water heater that's building up sediment. Caught now, those are quick, inexpensive fixes, and small leaks alone can quietly add to your water bill every month. Left alone, that same small stuff is what turns into water damage or the emergency call, and that never happens at a convenient time.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for yes.)

Since it's been a while, I'd suggest having us go through the plumbing in the home, the water heater, the drains, the shutoff valves, that way you know everything is in good shape, and if it all looks great, that's good news too.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

(Opportunities to note: whole-home plumbing inspection, water heater flush, maintenance agreement, main shutoff valve check.)

steps.title: Doesn’t Know When It Was Serviced
steps.content:
No problem, honestly, most people don't keep track of that. Plumbing is out of sight, out of mind until something goes wrong.

Can I share why I ask? (Wait for their response.)

Two reasons, really. Things like a slow drip or a running toilet quietly add to your water bill every single month. Money you're spending without getting anything for it. And the bigger one. When a plumber catches a small issue early, like a worn valve or a slow leak under a sink, it's usually a quick, inexpensive fix. It's the small stuff nobody catches that turns into water damage or the emergency call, and that never happens at a convenient time.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for yes.)

Since nobody's sure where things stand, I'd suggest having us give the plumbing a complete check, the water heater, the drains, the shutoff valves, that way you know exactly what shape everything is in, and if it all looks great, that's good news too.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

steps.title: The Maintenance Plan Pivot
steps.content:
That's great that you're staying on top of it, honestly, you're ahead of most people.

Can I share a thought? (Wait for their response.)

The hardest part of taking care of plumbing isn't the service itself. It's remembering to schedule it. Life gets busy, a year slips by, and that's usually when something small gets missed. The whole point of a regular plan is that you never have to remember. We remember for you, it stays on a consistent schedule, and small issues get caught while they're still quick, inexpensive fixes instead of water damage or emergency repairs.

Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for yes.)

Since you're already taking care of the home, it may make sense to have us handle the regular plumbing checks for you going forward. That way it's off your plate entirely.

Does that sound reasonable?

(Wait for the yes.)

Great, let me see what we have available.

(Opportunities to note: whole-home plumbing inspection, water heater flush, maintenance agreement, main shutoff valve check.)

steps.title: The Transition
steps.content: Well {{contact_first_name}}, that's exactly why I'm glad we connected today. Let me ask you a few quick questions so I can update your service records properly. Is that okay?

steps.title: Digging In: Update the Records
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, while I have you, let me just run through a few quick things so we have an accurate picture, okay?

(Ask about each one at a time, acknowledge briefly, and note which ones come up. Do not dig into any single one yet.)

How’s the hot water? Plenty for everyone, or does it run out faster than it used to?

Any drains that have gotten slow, or clogs that keep coming back?

Any faucets dripping, or toilets that run on their own?

Have you noticed the water bill creeping up without a reason?

How’s the water pressure? Strong everywhere, or weak in places?

How’s the water itself? Any taste, smell, or hard-water spots on dishes and fixtures?

If you have a sump pump, when’s the last time anyone checked it actually works?

Anything you’ve just been living with. A disposal that jams, a fixture you’ve been meaning to replace?

Recap and focus: So {{contact_first_name}}, it sounds like the biggest things are X, Y, and Z. Is that right? Of everything we just talked about, which one bothers you the most?

(Their answer is the heart of the call. Click the one they name.)

steps.title: Focus: Water Heater & Hot Water
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, that's the one we hear most, and nobody should be rationing hot water in their own house.

Quick question. Does it run out faster than it used to, take forever to warm up, or both? And do you happen to know how old the water heater is?

(Age matters a lot here. Note their answers for the plumber.)

steps.title: Focus: Drains & Sewer
steps.content:
I'm glad you mentioned that, {{contact_first_name}}. Here's the thing about clogs that keep coming back: the plunger is treating the symptom, not the cause. When the same drain clogs over and over, something further down the line is catching things, and it only builds.

Is it one drain, or more than one? And how often is it happening at this point?

(More than one drain, or sewage smells, can mean the main line. Note it. If sewage is backing up, use the URGENT button.)

steps.title: Focus: Leaks, Drips & Running Toilets
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, that little drip is quieter than it is cheap. A running toilet alone can waste two hundred gallons a day, and it all shows up on the water bill.

Which is it? A faucet dripping, a toilet running, or have you noticed the bill creeping up without knowing why?

(A rising bill with no visible leak can mean a hidden one. Note their answers.)

steps.title: Focus: Water Pressure & Aging Pipes
steps.content:
That's a really useful one to know, {{contact_first_name}}. Weak pressure is annoying, but it's also information, especially in an older home, it can mean the pipes themselves are narrowing from the inside.

Is it everywhere in the house, or just certain faucets? And do you happen to know how old the house's plumbing is?

(Whole-house pressure loss in an older home is worth a real look. Note their answers.)

steps.title: Focus: Water Quality
steps.content:
I'm glad you brought that up, {{contact_first_name}}. You use that water for everything: drinking, cooking, bathing the kids.

Is it more the taste or smell, or the hard-water side? Spots on the dishes, scale on the fixtures, soap that won't lather right?

(Hard water also quietly shortens the life of the water heater and fixtures. Note their answers.)

steps.title: Focus: Sump Pump
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I'm really glad you mentioned that. The thing about a sump pump is you only find out it's broken on the worst possible day, standing in a wet basement.

When's the last time anyone actually tested it? And does it have a battery backup for when storms knock the power out?

(A pump test is quick, and it's the cheapest flood insurance there is.)

steps.title: Focus: Fixtures, Disposal & Projects
steps.content:
That's great to know, {{contact_first_name}}, whether it's a disposal that's given up, a fixture that's past its prime, or a bathroom you've been dreaming about, that's exactly the kind of thing we love to help with.

Tell me a little more. What have you been living with, or what's the project?

(Note the details. Project conversations are appointments, not phone quotes.)

steps.title: Making It Real
steps.content:
(Take the concern they named and make it present with three questions, in order.)

How long has that been going on? A few weeks, a month or two?

Is it here and there, or is it pretty much every day at this point?

When it acts up, how does it affect things? The morning routine? The water bill? Worry about water damage? (Let them open up. Do not rush.)

Then respond with empathy: Thank you for sharing that. That makes complete sense, and that's exactly the kind of thing our plumbers help people with every single day.

steps.title: The Review & Bridge
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, let me make sure I've got this right. (Recap what they told you: how long, how often, and how it affects them.) Did I get that right?

And it sounds like what you'd really love is for the plumbing to just be something you never have to think about. Is that fair to say?

(Almost everyone says yes. That yes is the moment.)

steps.title: The Magic Question & Recommendation
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, here's how this works: one of our plumbers comes out, takes a look at it, and sees exactly what's going on. And while they're out there, they'll give the whole house’s plumbing a complete once-over, so if anything else is going on, you'll know about it before it becomes a problem. And if it all checks out great, we'll tell you that too. We're not here to waste your time or your money. Does that make sense?

(Wait for the yes.)

{{contact_first_name}}, can I make a recommendation?

(Wait for yes.)

Based on everything you've told me, my recommendation is that we get one of our plumbers out to take that look. Does that sound reasonable?

(Ask "does that sound reasonable", never "does that sound good." Click what you hear next.)

steps.title: Uncover the Real Concern
steps.content:
I understand, {{contact_first_name}}. Let me ask. What is it that would keep you from taking care of something you've told me is bothering you?

(Listen. Their real answer is almost always one of the buttons below.)

steps.title: Objection: Cost
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I completely understand. I want to be clear. This first step is simply having a plumber come take a look so you know exactly where things stand. You're not committing to anything today. And knowing is what protects you. It's the small stuff nobody catches that turns into the expensive problem later.

(Do NOT improvise pricing or discounts on the call. Let the office handle specifics.)

Confirm and continue: Does that make sense? (Wait for a fast yes.) Do you have any other questions or concerns?

steps.title: Objection: “I need to think about it”
steps.content:
That's completely fair, {{contact_first_name}}. Can I ask what part you'd want to think over? Sometimes it's the cost, sometimes it's the timing, and sometimes people just aren't sure it's worth a visit, which one is closest for you?

(Listen, their answer usually turns into one of the other buttons. If it stays vague, continue below.)

The nice thing is, the visit is just information. You'll know exactly what shape the plumbing is in, and then you can think it over with real answers instead of guesses.

Confirm and continue: Does that make sense? (Wait for a fast yes.) Do you have any other questions or concerns?

steps.title: Objection: “I need to talk to my spouse”
steps.content:
That makes complete sense, {{contact_first_name}}. What most people find helpful is having the plumber take a look first. That way you'll both have real information to decide with, instead of guessing.

Confirm and continue: Does that make sense? (Wait for a fast yes.) Do you have any other questions or concerns?

steps.title: Objection: “I’m too busy / no time”
steps.content:
I completely understand, {{contact_first_name}}. Life gets busy. The nice thing is, you don't have to do anything for this one: our plumber does the work, and we'll schedule it around whatever works for you.

Confirm and continue: Does that make sense? (Wait for a fast yes.) Do you have any other questions or concerns?

steps.title: “Not Interested”
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. I'm not calling to sell you anything today. We're just updating our records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and {{practice_name}} wanted to make sure the plumbing is still treating you right. Can I ask just one quick question? Is everything still running the way it should?

(A genuine question, asked warmly, re-opens most of these calls. Click what you hear.)

steps.title: Scheduling: Two Yes-Yes Options
steps.content:
Wonderful, {{contact_first_name}}. {{rec_pronoun_cap}} have time this week on (day) and (day). Do mornings or afternoons work better for you?

(Let them answer.)

Perfect, I have a (time) and a (time) available, which is better?

(Let them answer.)

Great, I've got you down for (day) at (time).

(Always offer two yes-yes options within 48 hours. Before the call, know your two days and two times so you can fill these in without hesitating. Click what happens next.)

steps.title: Confirming the Appointment
steps.content:
Perfect, {{contact_first_name}}. Let me just confirm a couple of quick things: the best number to reach you is the one I called, right? And the address we have on file is still current? Great, and will you be home for the visit, or should the plumber plan to meet someone else?

(Confirm phone, address, and who'll be there. Click what happens next.)

steps.title: Final Discovery
steps.content:
One last thing, {{contact_first_name}}. Besides what we talked about, is there anything else around the house you'd like the plumber to look at while they're out there? Anything at all, even little stuff you've been putting off?

(This is where extra value gets found. Note anything they mention for the visit.)

steps.title: Closing the Call: Appointment Set
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, you're all set for the visit. Our plumber will take a good look at everything, and like I said, if it all checks out great, that's exactly what we'll tell you. Thanks so much for the time today, and we'll see you soon!

(Add your notes and press the green "Scheduled" button below to log the call.)

steps.title: Closing the Call: Callback Set
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. When would be a better time for me to give you a call back? (Pin down a real day and time, don't settle for "sometime.")

Perfect, I'll give you a call then. Thanks so much, and have a great rest of your day!

(Add your notes, then press "Spoke. Call back later" below and pick the date they gave you.)

steps.title: Closing the Call: Not Now
steps.content:
No problem at all, {{contact_first_name}}. I appreciate you taking the time today. If anything ever comes up with the plumbing, you know right where we are. Have a wonderful rest of your day!

(Add your notes and log the call with the disposition that fits.)

steps.title: Voicemail
steps.content:
Hi {{contact_first_name}}, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. We're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and I wanted to check in on your home's plumbing. Nothing urgent. I'd just love to make sure everything's still running the way it should. Please give me a call back at {{practice_phone}}. Again, this is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}} at {{practice_phone}}. Thanks, and have a great day!

(Press the "Voicemail" button below to log the call. The system will schedule the retry automatically.)

steps.title: Someone Else Answered
steps.content:
Oh hi. This is {{caller_name}} with {{practice_name}}. We're just updating our service records and I was hoping to catch {{contact_first_name}} for a quick minute. Are they around?

(If they ask what it's about: "We take care of the plumbing at the house, and we're just checking in on our customers." Warm, brief, no pitch to the gatekeeper.)

steps.title: “Why Are You Calling?” / “Is This Sales?”
steps.content:
That's a fair question, {{contact_first_name}}, and no, I'm not calling to sell you anything today. We're updating our service records on customers we haven't seen in a while, and {{practice_name}} asked me to check in and make sure the plumbing is still treating you right. That's really it. So, how has it been running?

(Honest, relaxed, no defensiveness. Click what you hear.)

steps.title: Service Recovery: They Weren’t Happy
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, I'm really sorry to hear that, and I'm glad you told me. Can I ask what happened? (Listen fully. Do not interrupt, do not defend. Let them get it all out, then:) Thank you for telling me that. I'm going to make sure {{practice_name}} hears about it personally.

{{contact_first_name}}, I know we can't undo that experience, but I'd love the chance to make it right. Would you be open to letting us take another look, and if you're not thrilled this time, you'll never hear from us again?

(A sincere apology plus a low-risk offer wins back more customers than any discount.)

steps.title: They Use Another Company Now
steps.content:
Oh, that's completely fair, {{contact_first_name}}. I'm glad you've got someone taking care of it. Can I ask, just for our records? Was there anything about your experience with us that made you switch? (Listen. If there was a problem, treat it as service recovery.)

Well, I appreciate the honesty. If anything ever changes, or you'd like a second opinion on a big repair, we'd love the chance to earn you back. Have a wonderful day!

steps.title: They Had the Plumbing Redone
steps.content:
Oh, that's great to hear, {{contact_first_name}}. New plumbing is a big investment in the house. Can I ask who did the work for you? (If it was us, celebrate it. If not, stay warm, no guilt.)

Even with new work, things like water heaters and drains still need an eye kept on them to protect that investment. Is anyone taking care of that for you?

(New work is a maintenance conversation, not a lost customer.)

steps.title: Moved, Renting, or Property Changes
steps.content:
Oh, thanks for letting me know, {{contact_first_name}}. Just so I update our records right. Did you move, or is the property being rented out now?

(If they moved: wish them well, ask if the new owner might want our info, and log the call. If they're the landlord: they still own the plumbing. Continue the conversation about keeping it in good shape between tenants.)

steps.title: Wrong Number
steps.content:
Oh, I apologize for the confusion. I was trying to reach {{contact_first_name}}. Sorry to bother you, and have a great day!

(Log the call with a note that the number is wrong so we don't call it again.)

steps.title: “Don’t Call Me Again”
steps.content:
I completely understand, and I'll make sure of it right now. You won't hear from us again. Thank you for your time, and have a good day.

(Press the "Do Not Call" button below immediately. This is a legal requirement, not a judgment call.)

steps.title: URGENT: Safety First
steps.content:
{{contact_first_name}}, stop me right there. Let's take care of you first.

If you smell gas: please hang up with me, get everyone out of the house, and call your gas company's emergency line or 911 right away.

If sewage is backing up or water is actively flooding: shut off the main water valve if you can get to it safely, and let's get a plumber out to you as an emergency call. Today.

(Follow your company's emergency dispatch procedure. Do not continue the reactivation script.)
